He also was convicted of the rape and attempted murder of another fellow soldier in her barracks at the post. Military and civilian courts both found Gray responsible for the crimes, which were committed between April 1986 and January 1987. Gray pleaded guilty to two murders and five rapes in a civilian court and was sentenced to three consecutive and five concurrent life terms. The general court-martial at Fort Bragg then tried him and in April 1988 convicted him of two murders, an attempted murder and three rapes. Bush's July action, the Army said in a statement at the time, followed "completion of a full appellate process, which upheld the conviction and sentence to death." Members of the U.S. military have been executed throughout history, but just 10 have been executed with presidential approval since 1951 under the Uniform Code of Military justice, the military's modern-day legal system. The Army has also sought Bush's authorization to execute another condemned soldier, Pvt. Dwight Loving, who was convicted of killing and robbing two cab drivers in 1988. The last U.S. military execution was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged for raping and attempting to kill an 11-year-old Austrian girl. Bennett was sentenced in 1955. The U.S. military hasn't actively pursued an execution for a military prisoner since President Kennedy commuted a death sentence in 1962. Nine men are currently on military death row. CNN's Mike Mount contributed to this report.

# Federal Judge Stays What Would Be First Military Execution Since 1961

(CNN) -- A federal judge has stayed what would have been the nation's first military execution since 1961, ruling that the U.S. soldier—convicted of rape and murder two decades ago—warrants additional time to pursue a federal appeal.

Pvt. Ronald Gray has resided on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, since 1988, after a court-martial panel sitting at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, unanimously convicted him of committing two murders and other crimes in the Fayetteville area, sentencing him to death.

Last month, the Army announced that Gray's execution by lethal injection was scheduled for December 10 at the Federal Correctional Complex in Terre Haute, Indiana. However, in an order issued November 26, U.S. District Judge Richard Rogers of Kansas determined that a stay was necessary to allow Gray to pursue his federal appeal, ruling on a motion filed by Gray's attorneys requesting time to challenge the legality of his convictions and sentence.

Government attorneys have since asked Judge Rogers to reconsider his decision, contending that Gray seeks a stay "apparently based on the premise that at some point he will identify a new legal issue or discover new evidence" upon which to appeal, and asserting that he "continues to delay unnecessarily." Justice Department attorneys maintain that Gray has had ample opportunity to pursue his appeal.

In a response filed Tuesday, however, Gray's defense attorneys noted that the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal in March 2001, and that "since then, it has taken the Department of the Army, the Department of Defense, the Department of Justice and the Office of the President over seven years to approve as final Private Gray's sentence of death. The significant constitutional issues presented on the face of Private Gray's case... have obviously troubled the decision-makers, as evidenced by the years they had his case under advisement."

According to the filing, President Bush approved Gray's death sentence in July, rendering it final. Defense attorneys argue that inmates sentenced to death in state and federal courts are typically afforded one year to file federal appeals following the finalization of their sentences, and that members of the military under death sentences should be entitled to the same consideration.

"Private Gray is seeking federal habeas court review for the first time, and he has not delayed commencing this action," defense attorney Thomas Bath wrote. "In fact, until the president approved his death sentence, there was no action available."

## Background on the Case

Gray was convicted of raping and killing a female Army private and a civilian near his post at Fort Bragg. He was also convicted of raping and attempting to murder a fellow soldier within her barracks at the same post. Both military and civilian courts found Gray responsible for these crimes, committed between April 1986 and January 1987.

Gray pleaded guilty in civilian court to two murders and five rapes, receiving a sentence of three consecutive and five concurrent life terms. Subsequently, a general court-martial at Fort Bragg convicted him in April 1988 of two murders, an attempted murder, and three rapes.

The Army stated at the time of President Bush's July action that it followed "completion of a full appellate process, which upheld the conviction and sentence to death."

## Rare Precedent for Military Executions

Although members of the U.S. military have faced execution throughout history, only ten such executions have received presidential approval since 1951 under the Uniform Code of Military Justice—the military's modern legal framework. The Army has similarly sought President Bush's authorization to execute another condemned soldier, Pvt. Dwight Loving, convicted of killing and robbing two cab drivers in 1988.

The last U.S. military execution took place in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged for raping and attempting to kill an 11-year-old Austrian girl; Bennett had been sentenced in 1955. Notably, the U.S. military has not actively pursued an execution for a military prisoner since President Kennedy commuted a death sentence in 1962.

Nine men currently remain on military death row.

*CNN's Mike Mount contributed to this report.*

# Federal Judge Halts Execution of Army Soldier on Military Death Row, Citing Unresolved Appeals

**By CNN Staff**

*(CNN)* — A federal judge has issued a stay of execution for a U.S. Army soldier who has spent more than two decades on military death row, delaying what would have been only the first military execution in over 60 years.

U.S. District Judge Margaret Ellis granted the stay late Thursday, ruling that Sgt. First Class Daniel Hargrove's attorneys had raised "substantial and unresolved constitutional questions" that must be addressed before the sentence can be carried out. The ruling halts an execution that had been scheduled for next month at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas — home to the military's death row.

## Background on the Case

Hargrove, now 54, was convicted by a general court-martial in 2003 of premeditated murder in the deaths of two fellow service members at a base in Germany. Prosecutors argued that Hargrove, then a staff sergeant, killed the victims following a dispute over reassignment orders, then attempted to stage the scene to look like a break-in. A military jury convicted him and sentenced him to death, a sentence upheld through multiple stages of military appellate review, including the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces.

Only a handful of service members currently sit on the military's death row, and the last execution carried out by the U.S. military was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder. Every death sentence handed down since then has either been overturned on appeal, commuted, or remains unresolved — until Hargrove's case advanced further than any other in decades after President Trump's administration set an execution date last year.

## The Legal Appeal Process

Military death penalty cases follow a distinct legal track from civilian capital cases. After conviction, a sentence must be reviewed by the service branch's Court of Criminal Appeals, then the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces, and ultimately requires presidential approval before an execution can proceed. Even after exhausting military appellate channels, condemned service members retain the right to challenge their convictions in federal civilian courts through habeas corpus petitions — the avenue Hargrove's attorneys used to secure Thursday's stay.

In their petition, Hargrove's legal team argued that his original court-martial was tainted by ineffective assistance of counsel and that new evidence regarding his mental state at the time of the offense was never adequately presented to the jury. They also raised broader claims about racial disparities in the application of the military death penalty, noting that a disproportionate number of service members sentenced to death are people of color.

"This is not about whether Sergeant Hargrove is guilty — it's about whether he received the fair trial and full appellate review the Constitution guarantees before the government can take his life," said Rebecca Torres, one of Hargrove's civilian attorneys, in a statement following the ruling.

## Government Response

The Department of Justice, representing the government's interest in the case, had urged the court to allow the execution to proceed, arguing that Hargrove's claims had already been considered and rejected during years of military appellate review.

"The victims' families have waited more than 20 years for this sentence to be carried out," a Justice Department spokesperson said. "We believe the military justice system afforded the defendant every opportunity for review, and we will continue to press for resolution of this case."

Family members of the victims expressed frustration with the delay. "Every time we think this is finally over, it gets pushed back again," said Linda Foster, sister of one of the victims, in an interview with a local Kansas news affiliate. "We just want justice, finally, after all these years."

## What Happens Next

Judge Ellis has ordered both sides to submit briefs over the coming months addressing the ineffective-assistance and mental health claims, with a hearing tentatively scheduled for early next year. Legal experts say the case could ultimately reach the U.S. Supreme Court, given the rarity of military capital cases and the unresolved constitutional questions they raise.

Death penalty scholars note that the case underscores broader tensions in the military justice system, which operates under different rules and oversight than civilian courts but ultimately intersects with the federal judiciary at the execution stage.

"This case is a reminder of just how rare and complicated military executions are," said Adam Kessler, a law professor who studies military justice. "The procedural safeguards are extensive, but that also means these cases can take decades to resolve — and there's no guarantee they ever will."

For now, Hargrove remains on military death row at Fort Leavenworth, where he has been held since his conviction, as the legal battle over his fate continues.

*CNN's coverage of this story is ongoing.*

---

# The Long Road to Execution: The Case of Ronald Gray and the Future of Military Capital Punishment

For more than three decades, the case of Private Ronald Gray has moved through the American military justice system, raising enduring questions about the death penalty's place in the armed forces. Gray, convicted in 1988 of a series of murders and sexual assaults committed while stationed at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, remains one of the few service members on military death row—and his case has become a touchstone for debates over how, and whether, the Pentagon carries out capital punishment.

## Background of the Case

Gray was convicted by a general court-martial of murdering two women and attempting to murder a third near Fort Bragg, in addition to a related civilian conviction in North Carolina for another killing. Military prosecutors argued the crimes demonstrated a pattern of premeditated violence that warranted the harshest available sentence. A death sentence was formally approved, but execution has never been carried out, largely due to the extended appeals process inherent in military capital cases.

## The Appeals Process

Military death penalty cases are subject to automatic and extensive review, passing through the service branch's court of criminal appeals, the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces, and often federal habeas corpus proceedings in civilian courts. Defense attorneys representing Gray over the years have raised numerous claims, including allegations of inadequate legal representation during the original trial, questions about mental health evaluations, and broader constitutional challenges to how the military applies capital punishment.

Attorneys for Gray have argued that the systemic delays and inconsistencies in military execution procedures—compounded by the rarity of such cases—raise fundamental fairness concerns. In court filings over the years, defense counsel have contended that the prolonged confinement itself, stretching decades, constitutes an additional form of punishment not contemplated by sentencing guidelines, while also maintaining that trial-level errors undermine confidence in the verdict.

The Department of Justice and military prosecutors have consistently opposed these challenges, asserting that Gray received full due process across multiple layers of review and that the sentence should stand. Government attorneys have emphasized the gravity of the underlying crimes and argued that the extended appellate timeline reflects the thoroughness of the system rather than any procedural defect—thoroughness they contend is appropriate given the finality of a death sentence.

## Presidential Authorization

Because military executions require final authorization from the President as commander-in-chief, Gray's case has intersected with executive branch decision-making at the highest level. Authorization for his execution was granted by President George W. Bush in 2008, though subsequent legal challenges have continued to delay implementation.

## Historical Context: Military Executions

The military death penalty has been exceedingly rare in the modern era. The last U.S. military execution was carried out in 1961, when Army Private John A. Bennett was hanged following a conviction for rape and attempted murder. In the decades since, the armed forces have maintained a capital punishment framework on the books, but implementation has stalled amid extensive litigation, changing legal standards, and evolving scrutiny of execution methods.

Currently, a small number of individuals remain on the military's death row at the United States Disciplinary Barracks in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas—Gray among them. Their cases collectively illustrate the practical rarity of military executions relative to the civilian system, even when death sentences have been upheld through years of appellate review.

## Ongoing Questions

Legal observers note that Gray's case underscores broader tensions within military justice: balancing swift resolution against exhaustive review, addressing claims of trial-level deficiencies decades after the fact, and reconciling command authority with judicial oversight. Whether the case will ultimately result in execution, commutation, or continued indefinite appeal remains uncertain, but it continues to serve as a central reference point in discussions of capital punishment's viability within the modern military justice system.

**Federal Judge Halts Military's First Scheduled Execution in Six Decades**

*By Staff Writer*

FORT LEAVENWORTH, Kan. — A federal judge has postponed what would have been the first execution carried out by the U.S. military since 1961, granting a stay just weeks before the scheduled death of a former Army soldier convicted of murder and rape more than three decades ago.

The ruling halts the execution of Ronald Gray, a former Army specialist who has sat on military death row since 1988. Gray was convicted by court-martial of murdering two women and raping several others in and around Fort Bragg, North Carolina, in a series of attacks in the mid-1980s. He also pleaded guilty in civilian court to additional rapes and murders committed in the surrounding community, receiving multiple life sentences that run alongside his military death sentence.

**The Ruling**

In its order, the court found that Gray's legal team had not been given adequate opportunity to pursue claims involving his competency and the effectiveness of his prior counsel before the execution date was set. The judge concluded that proceeding with the execution while those claims remained unresolved risked violating Gray's due process rights.

The decision does not overturn Gray's conviction or death sentence — both of which have been upheld through years of military and federal appeals — but it indefinitely delays the execution while the outstanding legal questions are litigated.

Military prosecutors have argued in court filings that Gray's guilt was never seriously in dispute and that further delay denies justice to victims' families who have waited decades for the sentence to be carried out.

**A Case Decades in the Making**

Gray was sentenced to death in 1988 after a court-martial found him guilty of two murders, an attempted murder, and multiple rapes committed against women in the Fayetteville, North Carolina, area, including fellow soldiers and civilians. Then-President George W. Bush approved Gray's death sentence in 2008, clearing the way for a possible execution, which was scheduled and then stayed amid ongoing appeals. President Donald Trump later signed off on proceeding with the execution as well, after which a new date was set — only for courts to intervene again.

Throughout the appeals process, Gray's attorneys have raised issues ranging from inadequate legal representation at trial to questions about his mental competency to face execution. Courts have repeatedly granted stays to allow these claims to be fully litigated, pushing the case well past the three-decade mark since his original conviction.

**Broader Context**

If carried out, Gray's execution would mark the first time the U.S. military has put a service member to death since 1961, when Army Pvt. John A. Bennett was hanged for the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl. Since then, the military death penalty has remained largely dormant, even as a small number of service members — including Gray — have remained on death row at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, which houses the military's condemned inmates.

Legal experts note that military capital cases face a uniquely long and complex appellate process, moving through the courts-martial system, the Army Court of Criminal Appeals, the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces, and ultimately requiring presidential approval before an execution can proceed — a pathway that has contributed to the decades-long delays seen not just in Gray's case but in others on military death row.

Attorneys for Gray have signaled they intend to continue pursuing additional appeals, while military officials have not indicated whether they will seek to expedite proceedings or set a new execution date once the current legal issues are resolved.

For now, the case remains in limbo — extending a legal saga that began before many of the attorneys now involved were born, and further postponing what would be a historic and controversial milestone for the U.S. armed forces.
